lesson.title: The Multimeter: One Tool, Three Measurements
lesson.summary: A multimeter combines a voltmeter, an ammeter, and an ohmmeter into a single handheld instrument, and using the correct mode and connection method for each is essential to measuring voltage, current, and resistance correctly.
lesson.body:
A multimeter is built around one sensitive measurement core that, through internal switching, added resistors, and shunts, can be reconfigured to measure voltage, current, or resistance, the same three quantities you have already studied, all from a single pair of test leads and one mode dial. Selecting the wrong mode for what you are trying to measure is one of the most common mistakes made with this tool, so it is worth being precise about how each mode actually connects to a circuit.

To measure voltage, connect the meter in parallel across the two points you care about. Voltage is a difference between two points, so the meter simply listens in across that gap without needing to become part of the current path itself. To measure current, the meter must instead be placed in series, meaning you physically break the circuit at some point and force the current to flow directly through the meter, since current is the flow through a single path and there is no other way to measure all of it. To measure resistance, the component generally needs to be powered off, and often disconnected from the rest of the circuit entirely, because the meter measures resistance by pushing its own small, known test current through the component and reading the resulting voltage; any outside voltage or parallel current path would corrupt that reading.

Here is a worked example that also demonstrates how the meter's own resistance mode works internally. A multimeter set to current mode, connected in series with a resistor, reads 3 mA, that is, 0.003 A, of current flowing. The same multimeter, moved to voltage mode and connected in parallel across that same resistor, reads 9 V. Using Ohm's law, R = V divided by I, gives R = 9 divided by 0.003, which equals 3000 ohms, or 3 kΩ. That two step measurement, current then voltage, is essentially what an ohmmeter mode does automatically in one step, just with the roles of known and measured quantities reversed: it supplies a known current and reads the resulting voltage.

One detail is especially relevant given everything covered in this chapter sequence: how a multimeter handles AC signals. Many of the signals discussed throughout this sequence, clipped waveforms, tones with added harmonic distortion, random noise, are not clean sine waves. An older or less expensive multimeter's AC voltage mode is often average responding, meaning it is internally calibrated assuming a pure sine wave shape in order to convert its reading into an RMS value. Feed it a distorted or clipped waveform, and that sine wave assumption breaks down, producing a measurably incorrect RMS reading. A true RMS multimeter instead computes the actual root mean square value of whatever waveform it is given, regardless of shape, which is why a true RMS meter is the correct tool for measuring the kinds of noisy, distorted, and clipped signals described throughout this chapter sequence, situations where an average responding meter can read noticeably wrong values.
